channel.title: Archetype Original
channel.description: Essays on leadership, culture, and accountability by Bart Paden.

item.title: The Account Under Fire
item.description: Part 3 closed on a warning. Everything built at Southwest or inside an Alcoa smelting plant got built with time. Years of consistent choices, banked one at a time, until people believed the standard was real. The next environment doesn't have that kind of time.

item.title: The Daniel Archetype
item.description: Daniel was taken to Babylon as a captive, one of the young men selected from Judah's nobility to be trained for service in Nebuchadnezzar's court.

item.title: Twenty Points Apart
item.description: Gallup asked leaders to rate themselves on seven leadership competencies. Then they asked the managers who work for those leaders to rate the same people on the same seven things.

item.title: The Jezebel Archetype
item.description: Jezebel never drew a sword. She wrote letters in the king's name, called an assembly, seated false witnesses, and let the process do the killing. The seventh Archetype entry on power that hides inside procedure.

item.title: The Signal I Was Actually Watching
item.description: A mentor client asked me whether there was a moment I knew I had made it, and he meant financially. There was no number. What I actually watched was whether my people were growing.

item.title: The Standard That Held
item.description: Nick Saban walked off the field for the last time in January 2024, and the word reporters kept reaching for was not relief. It was grief. Men who had been screamed at in practice did not describe a tyrant.

item.title: Unity Is Not Sameness
item.description: The growth of humans is tied to being united with others who are not the same. Most leaders agree with that in principle, then build a team that violates it in practice.

item.title: The Ruth Archetype
item.description: Naomi told both of her daughters-in-law to go home. She had nothing left to offer them: her husband dead, both sons dead, and a road back to a country that had watched her leave during a famine. Ruth refused to go.

item.title: Scoreboard Leadership
item.description: Wells Fargo's "Eight is Great" sales culture shows what happens when a number replaces a mission -- and why the two employees who used the company's own ethics hotline to report the fraud were the ones who got fired, years before Congress ever questioned the CEO who built it.

item.title: The Barnabas Archetype
item.description: Barnabas gave before proof existed: money, reputation, and a decade of belief in Paul with no contact to back it up. A positive archetype in the leadership series, examined through the same lens as Judas, Absalom, and Nehemiah.

item.title: They Still Call Him
item.description: Part one of a five-part series on transformational and servant leadership. Nick Saban's 1998 phone call to a stranger, days before the biggest game of his career, is the proof that transactional leadership fails under real pressure and what has to replace it.

item.title: The Absalom Archetype
item.description: Absalom never accused David of failing. He just stood in a gap his father left open, morning after morning, until the sympathy he built there cost David his own most trusted counselor.

item.title: The Pipeline Isn't Draining. It's Refusing to Fill.
item.description: Leadership burnout data reveals a pipeline collapse, not a wellness problem. When leaders exceed their capacity to absorb pressure, it goes downward onto teams or inward onto their own health. The next generation is watching and refusing to inherit the role under current conditions.

item.title: The Nehemiah Archetype
item.description: The wall was never the hardest part. Nehemiah held two threats at once, external opposition and corruption inside his own community, without letting either one wait.

item.title: The Data Caught Up
item.description: New research confirms what Holding the Line already argued: unenforced standards don't stay neutral, they quietly become the culture.

item.title: The Saul Archetype
item.description: Saul was chosen, transformed, and given every advantage a leader could ask for. His fall came from what he chose to protect once he had power, not from how he started. The third entry in The Archetype Series traces the decisions that took him from anointed to unrecognizable.

item.title: DARVO: When the Guilty Become the Victim
item.description: DARVO is a pattern used by offenders to deny behavior, attack the challenger, and reverse victim and offender roles. This entry examines how it works, why servant leaders are the specific target, the systems that make it sustainable, and what institutional courage actually requires.

item.title: The Joseph Archetype
item.description: The Joseph Archetype is the story of a leader who absorbed betrayal, stayed faithful in obscurity, and arrived at power without bitterness in the hand that held it. The second entry in The Archetype Series.

item.title: Power vs. Authority: Part 3 — The Test
item.description: What separates power from authority when something goes wrong. Crisis and pressure are the only real diagnostic. Power relies on the org chart when it needs people most. Authority calls and people show up.

item.title: Power vs. Authority: Part 2 — The Build
item.description: Most writing on earning authority makes it sound like a program. The build is not a program. It is a direction held under pressure, repeatedly, over enough time that the people around you stop waiting for the exception.

item.title: The Judas Archetype
item.description: The Judas Archetype is not a story about a monster. It is a story about a pattern. One that does not begin with betrayal. It ends there. And the path between the beginning and the end looks, for most of its length, like ordinary leadership behavior.

item.title: The System Behind the Conditions
item.description: Seven conditions. Eight posts. One question that has been building from the beginning. If these conditions matter, and the evidence says they do, how do you actually measure them honestly from both sides of the leadership relationship?

item.title: Power vs. Authority: Part 1 — The Hunger
item.description: The pursuit of power and the earning of authority look identical from the outside at first. Both involve influence. Both involve people following a direction. The difference lives underneath, in motive, in method, and in what survives. Part 1 of this series examines the hunger that precedes power, where it comes from, what it costs the person chasing it, and what it leaves behind in the people who were close enough to watch.

item.title: Affinity Dressed as Service
item.description: The leader most likely to miss favoritism is not the tyrant. It is the relational leader, the one who genuinely invests in people and believes deeply that their job is to serve. This entry examines how affinity masquerades as servant leadership and what Greenleaf's original test demands of every leader who claims the title.

item.title: The 7 Conditions: Drift
item.description: Drift is not a failure. It is the direction failure travels in when no one is watching closely enough. It is measurable, predictable, and almost always well underway before the people responsible for fixing it know it exists.

item.title: The 7 Conditions: Stability
item.description: Stability is not the absence of pressure. It is whether the environment holds under it. A stable organization can absorb difficulty without lurching. An unstable one cannot, and the people inside it spend more energy bracing than building.

item.title: The Approval Economy
item.description: When favoritism takes hold inside a team, something predictable happens. People stop optimizing for results and start optimizing for access. This entry examines how that shift happens, what it does to team culture, and why servant leadership demands a different economy entirely.

item.title: The Invisible Tax
item.description: Favoritism doesn't announce itself. It moves through an organization quietly, below the visible line of leadership behavior, and by the time the damage is measurable, it has already been paid for. This entry examines how favoritism forms, what it costs, and why the first condition for fixing it is being willing to look.

item.title: The 7 Conditions: Alignment
item.description: Alignment is not agreement in a meeting. It is whether the organization is actually moving in the same direction when leadership is not in the room. Most organizations have the appearance of alignment. Very few have the substance of it.

item.title: The 7 Conditions: Trust
item.description: Trust is not a feeling. It is the conclusion a team draws from a pattern they have been watching for months. It cannot be declared, mandated, or assumed. It is built through behavior or it does not exist at all.

item.title: The 7 Conditions: Consistency
item.description: Consistency is not about being the same person every day. It is about whether the people on your team can predict what you stand for, what you will enforce, and how you will show up when it costs you something.

item.title: The 7 Conditions: Communication
item.description: Communication is not whether the leader talks. It is whether the message arrives. The gap between what was sent and what was received is where organizations lose decisions, lose time, and lose people.

item.title: The 7 Conditions: Clarity
item.description: Clarity is not the certainty a leader feels. It is whether the people on their team actually know what matters, right now, in the work they are doing today. The gap between those two things is where organizations quietly lose.

item.title: The 7 Conditions: Why This Series Exists
item.description: We are going to spend the next seven posts talking about the conditions that determine whether your leadership is actually working. Not whether you think it is working. Whether the people living inside the system you have built experience it as working.

item.title: Are You a Leader Who Puts Your Words Into Action?
item.description: Servant leadership is not measured in declarations. It is measured in days. A look at what congruence actually costs, why the leader who has never failed is the most dangerous kind, and what it means to put your words into action.

item.title: Toxic Empathy Post 5: The Conversation
item.description: A practical look at what it actually means to lead through difficult conversations, how clarity is established in real time, and why holding both empathy and responsibility is what moves people and systems forward.

item.title: Toxic Empathy Post 4: Servant Leadership Role
item.description: A correction of servant leadership as a disciplined practice, clarifying the difference between empathy that serves and empathy that avoids responsibility, and how leaders must hold both awareness and accountability at the same time.

item.title: Toxic Empathy Post 3: The Cost of Avoidance
item.description: An examination of what actually happens when leaders avoid necessary action, how behavior is shaped through response, and how unaddressed issues compound into system-wide consequences over time.

item.title: Toxic Empathy Post 2: Holding the Line
item.description: A close examination of the exact moment leaders hesitate, why the decision to hold the line is difficult, and how avoiding that cost reshapes standards, effort, and culture in real time.

item.title: Toxic Empathy
item.description: An examination of toxic empathy in leadership, how avoidance disguises itself as care, and why servant leadership requires the strength to hold both presence and accountability.

item.title: Leading Well Under Bad Leadership
item.description: The final entry in the Unaccountable Leadership series examining how leaders maintain integrity and influence when the system above them refuses accountability.

item.title: Build It On Purpose
item.description: Reflections from a talk given to first-generation college-bound students on purpose, discipline, curiosity, failure, and why the real legacy isn’t what you build, but who you help become better.

item.title: Accountability Is a Design Problem
item.description: Post 8 of the Unaccountable series examines why goodwill and culture alone cannot sustain accountability, and why healthy leadership systems must design structural correction into authority itself.

item.title: Why Servant Leadership Disrupts Unaccountable Power
item.description: Post 7 of the Unaccountable series marks the pivot from diagnosis to disruption, examining how Servant Leadership restores consequence to insulated systems and exposes authority that cannot survive accountability.

item.title: The Distraction Play
item.description: Narcissistic leaders keep teams busy with noise to avoid accountability. Servant leaders resist constant pivots and focus attention on what truly matters.

item.title: After the Smoke Clears
item.description: A conclusion to the Narcissistic Leadership Tactics series, shifting focus from unhealthy patterns to the posture and practices of healthy, servant leadership.

item.title: How Pressure Triggers Threat in Unaccountable Leaders
item.description: An applied neuroscience examination of why ordinary accountability demands are processed as threat by unaccountable leaders, and how power, nervous system adaptation, and control shape leadership behavior.

item.title: How Unaccountable Leadership Becomes Structural
item.description: An editorial examination of how unaccountable leadership endures, not through personality, but through systems that reorganize to protect authority from consequence.

item.title: Recognizing Unsafe Leadership Environments
item.description: Post 9 of the Unaccountable series examines how unsafe leadership environments reveal themselves through patterns that restrict correction, narrow truth, and reorganize systems around protecting authority.

item.title: When Responsibility Stops Being Accidental
item.description: A research-informed editorial on what happens when leaders refuse accountability, how pressure gets redirected downward, harm becomes intentional, and teams absorb consequences leaders won’t own.
